```{r linear-mixed-models-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
library(car)
library(DHARMa)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(emmeans)
library(performance)
library(patchwork)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
options(scipen = 999)  # no sci notation

u_df <- read_csv("data/andrew.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  # Map to Quinn & Keough's Table 9.1 densities. NOTE the file's dens_33 /
  # dens_66 labels are the reverse of the book's percentages -- verified by
  # matching patch means: dens_33 is the book's 66% group, dens_66 its 33%.
  mutate(treat = case_when(
           treat == "removal" ~ "0%",     # book   0% density, mean algae 39.2
           treat == "dens_66" ~ "33%",    # book  33% density, mean algae 19.0
           treat == "dens_33" ~ "66%",    # book  66% density, mean algae 21.6
           treat == "control" ~ "100%"),  # book 100% density, mean algae  1.3
         treat = factor(treat, levels = c("0%", "33%", "66%", "100%")),
         patch = as_factor(patch))

u_summary <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(algae), sd = sd(algae),
            se = sd / sqrt(n), min = min(algae), max = max(algae))
```

## Where We Left Off

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Last week: **generalized** linear models. We changed the
**distribution** of the response (Poisson, binomial).

This week we change something else: **which observations are allowed
to count as independent**.

Today's plan:

1. Why quadrats in a patch are **not** independent replicates
2. Fit a **mixed model** and read its output
3. The **ICC**: how much of the variation is among patches
4. Test, check and report the result
5. The same ideas on the **crayfish**, **chicks** and **streams**
::::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**✅ Two words to keep straight all lecture**

R prints two variances. We will call them by R's names every time:

- **patch variance**: how much **patches** differ from each other
  (among-patch)
- **residual variance**: how much **quadrats** differ inside one patch
  (within-patch)
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Want the theory?**

How REML finds those variances, and where the *p*-values come from, is
in the
[Mixed Models Under the Hood](../../vignettes/16_lmm_under_the_hood_vignette/lmm_under_the_hood.qmd)
vignette. Optional.
:::
:::
::::::

## Part 1 · Why a One-Way ANOVA Fails These Data {.divider}

## The Data and the Design {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
`treat`: urchin density (0 / 33 / 66 / 100% of natural)
`patch`: 16 patches of reef, **4 per treatment**
`quad`: 5 quadrats scored inside every patch
`algae`: % cover of filamentous algae, the response

```{r linear-mixed-models-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_summary %>%
  dplyr::select(treat, n, mean, sd) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))
```

The design is **nested**:
treatment → patch → quadrat. Patch 7 is in one treatment only.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 The giveaway question**

***"What did I apply the treatment to?"***

The urchin density was set for a whole **patch**. So count patches:
**16**, not 80 quadrats.
:::

::: callout-important
**⚠️ So what is *n*?**

The 5 quadrats in a patch are **subsamples** of that patch, not 5
replicates of the treatment.

Treating all 80 quadrats as independent replicates is
**pseudoreplication** (Hurlbert 1984), the most common fatal flaw in
ecological statistics.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Levels in One Picture

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r lmm-levels-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Algae cover plotted for each of the sixteen patches, grouped into four panels by urchin density. Grey dots are the eighty quadrats, blue diamonds are the sixteen patch means, and an orange horizontal line in each panel is the treatment mean. Patch means scatter widely around their treatment line."
lv_patch <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(patch_mean = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

lv_treat <- lv_patch %>%
  group_by(treat) %>%
  summarise(treat_mean = mean(patch_mean), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(u_df, aes(patch, algae)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.2,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_point(data = lv_patch, aes(y = patch_mean),
             colour = "#0072B2", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  geom_hline(data = lv_treat, aes(yintercept = treat_mean),
             colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_grid(. ~ treat, scales = "free_x", switch = "x") +
  labs(x = "Patch, grouped by urchin density", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
Every quadrat's algae cover is three things added together:

1. its **treatment mean**: the [orange line]{style="color:#D55E00"}
2. how far its **patch** sits from that line: orange line to
   [blue diamond]{style="color:#0072B2"}. The spread of these is the
   **patch variance**.
3. how far the **quadrat** sits from its patch: blue diamond to grey
   dot. The spread of these is the **residual variance**.

::: callout-important
**That sentence is the whole model**

The treatment was applied to patches, so the treatment has to beat
piece 2, **patch-to-patch** scatter, not piece 3.

Keep this picture in mind. We come back to it when we read the output.
:::
:::
:::::

## Pseudoreplication, Priced {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
Same 80 numbers, two analyses:

``` r
# ignores patch: 80 quadrats treated as replicates
anova(lm(algae ~ treat, data = u_df))

# tests treatment against patches (the 1960s way)
aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch), data = u_df)
```

```{r lmm-pseudo-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
ps_naive  <- anova(lm(algae ~ treat, data = u_df))
ps_nested <- summary(aov(algae ~ treat + Error(patch),
                         data = u_df))[["Error: patch"]][[1]]

data.frame(
  analysis = c("Ignore patch", "Test against patches"),
  F        = round(c(ps_naive["treat", "F value"],
                     ps_nested["treat", "F value"]), 2),
  den_df   = c(ps_naive["Residuals", "Df"], ps_nested["Residuals", "Df"]),
  p        = c(format(round(ps_naive["treat", "Pr(>F)"], 5), scientific = FALSE),
               round(ps_nested["treat", "Pr(>F)"], 3)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**Same data: *p* = 0.00003 or *p* = 0.091**

Ignoring patch uses **76** denominator df, as if there were 80
independent replicates. Testing against patches uses **12**: 16
patches minus 4 treatments.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 What pseudoreplication does**

Both analyses see the **same big difference** in the treatment means
(39% vs 1%). Pseudoreplication does not invent the effect. It invents
**certainty**.
:::

The `Error(patch)` trick works, but only on balanced designs, and it
tells you nothing about the patches themselves. **That is what the
mixed model replaces.**
:::
:::::

## What If Urchins Did Nothing at All?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{r lmm-sim-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Two histograms of p-values from one thousand simulated experiments with no treatment effect. Ignoring patch, the leftmost bar below 0.05 holds about half of all experiments. With the mixed model the histogram is flat and the bar below 0.05 holds about five percent."
set.seed(2026)
sim_reef <- function() {
  d <- expand_grid(treat = factor(1:4), p = 1:4, q = 1:5) %>%
    mutate(patch = interaction(treat, p))
  d$y <- 30 + rnorm(16, 0, 17)[as.integer(d$patch)] + rnorm(80, 0, 17)
  c(naive = anova(lm(y ~ treat, data = d))[1, "Pr(>F)"],
    mixed = suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(
      anova(lmer(y ~ treat + (1 | patch), data = d))[1, "Pr(>F)"])))
}
sim_p  <- as_tibble(t(replicate(1000, sim_reef())))
sim_fp <- round(100 * colMeans(sim_p < 0.05))

sim_p %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "model", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(model = if_else(
    model == "naive",
    paste0("Ignore patch: ", sim_fp["naive"], "% false alarms"),
    paste0("Mixed model: ", sim_fp["mixed"], "% false alarms"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = p < 0.05), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05),
                 colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey70", "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "p-value for treatment", y = "Simulated experiments") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
1000 made-up reefs, laid out like the real one: 4 treatments, 4
patches each, 5 quadrats each, with the same patch and quadrat scatter.
**The treatment does nothing in any of them.**

A fair test should cry wolf 5% of the time.

::: callout-important
**Ignoring patch cries wolf about half the time**

Each treatment mean is an average of only **4 patches**, and patches
differ a lot. So even with no effect, the four means differ. Judge that
against quadrat noise and it looks far too big to be chance.
:::

The mixed model on the right is what we build next.
:::
:::::

## Part 2 · The Mixed Model and Its Output {.divider}

## What Makes an Effect "Random"?

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Ask one question: **do I care about these specific levels, or are they a
sample of levels I could have had?**

::: {.compact-table}
| | `treat` | `patch` |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| The levels are | 0/33/66/100% density | patches 1–16 |
| Chosen by | me, deliberately | whatever was there |
| Would a repeat study use the same ones? | **yes** | no, different patches |
| I want to estimate | **each level's mean** | **how much they vary** |
| So it is | **fixed** | **random** |
:::

::: callout-important
**The key consequence**

A random factor with 16 levels costs **one** number, the patch
variance, not 16 separate patch means.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 A useful test**

*"The 100% density treatment reduced algae"*: a reader cares about that
level. **Fixed.**

*"Patch 7 happened to be lush"*: nobody cares about patch 7 in
particular. **Random.**
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ You need enough levels**

A variance estimated from **fewer than ~5 levels** is unreliable. With
2 or 3 groups, fit them as fixed instead.

We have 16 patches, which is plenty. The crayfish (3 lakes) and streams
(3 streams) later show what too few costs.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Fitting It {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-05}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_lmer_model <- lmer(
  algae ~ treat + (1 | patch),
  data = u_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
```

Read the formula as:

```
algae  ~  treat      +   (1 | patch)
  ↑         ↑                ↑
response  fixed effect   random effect
```

**`(1 | patch)`**: the `1` is the **intercept**. Each patch gets its
own baseline algae cover. This is a **random intercept**.

`calc.derivs = FALSE` just skips a noisy convergence check. It does not
change the fit.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The model in symbols, then in words:

$$algae_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + b_{j(i)} + \epsilon_{ijk}$$

- $\mu + \alpha_i$: the **treatment mean** (orange line)
- $b_{j(i)}$: how far patch *j* sits from **its own treatment's
  mean** (orange to blue). Their spread is the **patch variance**.
- $\epsilon_{ijk}$: how far quadrat *k* sits from **its own patch's
  mean** (blue to grey). Their spread is the **residual variance**.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Patch IDs must be unique**

Our patches are numbered 1–16, so `(1 | patch)` knows patch 7 is one
place. If they were numbered 1–4 *inside every treatment*, R would
think "patch 1" was the same place in all four. Then write
`(1 | treat:patch)`, which is always safe.
:::
:::
:::::

## Reading the Output {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-05b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
summary(u_lmer_model)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Random effects**: the new block, two rows:

- **`patch (Intercept)` 294.3**: the **patch variance**. How far
  patches sit from their **own treatment's** mean, pooled over all four
  treatments.
- **`Residual` 298.6**: the **residual variance**. How far quadrats
  sit from their **own patch's** mean.

**`groups: patch, 16`**: R knows there are 16 patches. That is the
replication for `treat`.

**Fixed effects**: **skip this table.** `treat1`, `treat2` and so on are
deviations from the grand mean, which is confusing. Get treatment
means from `emmeans()` instead (Part 4).

::: callout-important
**Back to the picture**

Orange line → blue diamond: **294**.
Blue diamond → grey dot: **299**.

About equal. Patches differ as much as quadrats do.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 3 · The ICC: How Much Do Patches Matter? {.divider}

## The ICC: Two Extremes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
$$ICC = \frac{\text{patch variance}}{\text{patch variance} + \text{residual variance}}$$

The share of the variation that is **among patches**. It asks: *if I
pick two quadrats from the same patch, how alike are they?*

**ICC near 0: patches don't matter** (made-up numbers, same treatment)

::: {.compact-table}
| | Quadrats | Patch mean |
|---|---|---|
| Patch A | 10, 30, 5, 25, 20 | 18 |
| Patch B | 22, 8, 28, 12, 20 | 18 |
:::

The patch means are the same. All the variation is quadrat to quadrat.
Knowing the patch tells you nothing, so the quadrats act like
independent replicates.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**ICC near 1: patch is everything**

::: {.compact-table}
| | Quadrats | Patch mean |
|---|---|---|
| Patch A | 5, 6, 5, 4, 5 | 5 |
| Patch B | 40, 41, 39, 40, 40 | 40 |
:::

Quadrats inside a patch are nearly identical. You measured the same
number 5 times, so each patch is really **one** data point.

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Where real data sit**

Somewhere in between. The closer to 1, the less each extra quadrat
tells you, and the more it matters that patches, not quadrats, are the
replicates.
:::
:::
:::::

## The ICC on the Real Reef {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
The 4 patches with urchins **removed** (0%), all given the **same**
treatment:

::: {.compact-table}
| Patch | Quadrats | Patch mean |
|---|---|---|
| 13 | 46, 44, 41, 29, 11 | 34 |
| 14 | 65, 55, 61, 74, 55 | 62 |
| 15 | 0, 5, 0, 0, 6 | **2** |
| 16 | 30, 82, 70, 27, 83 | 58 |
:::

- **Among patches, big:** same treatment, but patch 15 is nearly bare
  while patch 14 is at 62%. That's the patch variance.
- **Within patches, also big:** patch 16 runs from 27 to 83. That's
  the residual variance.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-04b}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
icc(u_lmer_model)
```

294 / (294 + 299) = **0.50**. Report the **adjusted** ICC. (The
unadjusted one also counts treatment differences in the denominator.)

::: callout-important
**ICC = 0.50: half the differences in algae cover come from *which
patch* a quadrat was in**

So quadrats from one patch are not independent. One bare patch like 15
drags down the whole 0% mean, and only **more patches** can average
that out. Five more quadrats in patch 15 would just confirm it's bare.
:::
:::
:::::

## R²: How Much Does Each Part Explain? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-r2-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
r2(u_lmer_model)
```

A mixed model explains variation in **two** ways, so it gets **two**
R² values (Nakagawa & Schielzeth 2013):

- **Marginal R²**: the **fixed** effects only (`treat`)
- **Conditional R²**: fixed **and** random effects (`treat` + `patch`)

```{r lmm-r2-02}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 1.5
#| fig-alt: "A single horizontal bar split into three parts showing how the variation in algae cover divides up: about 24 percent explained by urchin treatment, about 38 percent by which patch a quadrat was in, and about 38 percent left over as quadrat-to-quadrat noise."
u_r2 <- r2(u_lmer_model)
r2_split <- tibble(
  part  = factor(c("treatment", "patch", "residual (quadrats)"),
                 levels = c("residual (quadrats)", "patch", "treatment")),
  share = c(u_r2$R2_marginal,
            u_r2$R2_conditional - u_r2$R2_marginal,
            1 - u_r2$R2_conditional))

ggplot(r2_split, aes(x = share, y = "", fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(part, "\n", round(100 * share), "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 2.8,
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("treatment" = "#D55E00", "patch" = "#0072B2",
                               "residual (quadrats)" = "grey55"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  labs(x = "Share of the variation in algae cover", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**24% treatment, 38% patch, 39% left over**

- **Treatment** explains about **24%** of the variation in algae cover
  (marginal R²).
- Add **which patch** a quadrat was in and it's **62%** (conditional
  R²).
- The gap, 62 − 24 = **38%**, is the patch part. That is the
  **unadjusted ICC** that `icc()` printed.

**Patches explain more of the variation than the treatment does.**
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Report both, and say which is which**

"R² = 0.62" on its own overstates what the treatment did. R² is a
**description**, not a test: the *F*-test is still the test.

The adjusted ICC (0.50) is different again: the patch share of the
variation *left after* treatment.
:::
:::
:::::

## Use It to Price the Next Experiment {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
The two variances give the standard error of a treatment mean for
**any** design, before you get wet:

$$SE = \sqrt{\frac{\text{patch var}}{\text{patches}} + \frac{\text{residual var}}{\text{patches} \times \text{quadrats}}}$$

```{r lmm-design-01}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(u_lmer_model))
var_patch <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "patch"]
var_resid <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

se_mean <- function(patches, quads) {
  sqrt(var_patch / patches + var_resid / (patches * quads))
}

round(c(done_4x5   = se_mean(4, 5),
        quads_4x20 = se_mean(4, 20),
        patch_8x5  = se_mean(8, 5)), 2)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**More quadrats: 9.41 → 8.79. More patches: 9.41 → 6.65.**

Four times the quadrat work buys almost nothing. Twice the patches,
with *half* that work, buys a lot. With 4 patches the SE can never get
below √(294.3 / 4) = 8.58, however many quadrats you count.
:::

::: callout-note
**📖 This is what *p* = 0.091 means**

The experiment was not short of data. It was short of **patches**. The
*p*-value alone could never have told you that. The variance
components can.
:::
:::
:::::

## Partial Pooling: What Happens to Each Patch

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
The random effect also changes each patch's **estimate**.

```{r linear-mixed-models-04c}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: "Slope plot comparing each patch's raw observed mean algae cover to its shrunken mixed-model estimate, with lines joining the two; estimates move toward their treatment mean, and patches with more extreme raw means move furthest."
raw_means <- u_df %>%
  group_by(treat, patch) %>%
  summarise(raw = mean(algae), .groups = "drop")

raw_means$fitted <- predict(u_lmer_model,
                            newdata = raw_means[, c("treat", "patch")])

raw_means %>%
  pivot_longer(c(raw, fitted), names_to = "kind", values_to = "algae") %>%
  mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("raw", "fitted"),
                       c("raw patch mean", "model estimate"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(kind, algae, group = patch, color = treat)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Algae cover (%)", color = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 New word: shrinkage**

Every patch estimate is pulled part of the way **toward its treatment
mean**. The model treats an extreme patch average as partly real and
partly luck.

How far it pulls comes from the same two variances: big patch variance
→ trust each patch more; big residual variance → trust it less.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Why this is a feature**

A patch whose 5 quadrats landed high is probably *not* quite that
extreme. The next 5 would come back closer to average.

This is **partial pooling**, between "every patch is unrelated" and
"all patches are identical". Simulations with the true answer visible
are in the Under the Hood vignette.
:::
::::
:::::::

## Part 4 · Testing, Checking and Reporting {.divider}

## Testing the Treatment: Two Tests, Two Answers {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-06}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")
```

```{r linear-mixed-models-07}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
Anova(u_lmer_model, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "Chisq")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| Test | Statistic | *p* | at α = 0.05 |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| ***F*, Kenward-Roger df** | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72 | **0.091** | not significant |
| Wald χ² | χ²~3~ = 8.15 | 0.043 | significant |
:::

**Report the *F*-test.** Denominator df = **12** (16 patches − 4
treatments): it counts patches, just like `Error(patch)` did, and gives
the identical *p*.

The χ² assumes you have **infinite** replicates and that the two
variances are known exactly. With 16 patches, it is over-confident.

::: callout-warning
**🖐 The uncomfortable part**

Run only the χ² and you would report a significant effect and never
know. With few groups, which is nearly always in ecology, use the
***F*-test** and say which df method you used.
:::
:::
:::::

## Treatment Means and Post-Hoc Comparisons {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-09}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| collapse: true
u_emm <- emmeans(u_lmer_model, ~ treat)

multcomp::cld(u_emm, Letters = letters)
```

Every SE is **9.41**, on **12 df**: it comes from the **patches** (4
per treatment), not the 20 quadrats.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**Every treatment shares the letter `a`**

No pair is clearly different. That's expected: the overall *F*-test
was not significant (*p* = 0.091). Post-hocs after a non-significant
test are exploratory only.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Two intervals go below zero**

Algae cover can't be negative. The mixed model fixed the **error
structure** but still assumes a **normal** response. Last week fixed
the distribution. Real data often need both: `glmer()`, next.
:::
:::
:::::

## Diagnostics 1: Look With `check_model()` {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-12}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "The performance package's check_model output for the urchin mixed model, with three panels: a normal Q-Q plot of the residuals whose tails bend away from the line, a Q-Q plot of the sixteen patch random effects which sit close to their line, and a homogeneity-of-variance panel whose trend rises from left to right."
check_model(u_lmer_model,
            check = c("qq", "reqq", "homogeneity"))
```
:::

::::: {.column width="44%"}
The same call as every model this term, with **one new panel**.

::: callout-note
**📖 `reqq` is the new one**

A mixed model assumes **two** things are normal: the residuals *and the
random effects*. `reqq` is a Q-Q plot of the 16 patch intercepts.

They look fine, but it's only 16 points, so it can't support a strong
claim either way.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Skip the old residual tests here**

`check_normality()`, `check_heteroscedasticity()` and `leveneTest()`
all assume independent observations. On a mixed model they use the
wrong yardstick and shout *p* < 0.001. Use the plots to **look**, and
DHARMa (next) to **decide**.
:::
:::::
::::::

## Diagnostics 2: Decide With DHARMa {.tight-code}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-diag-03}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: "DHARMa diagnostic output for the urchin mixed model: a Q-Q plot of scaled residuals against a uniform reference with the KS, dispersion and outlier test results printed on it, beside a plot of scaled residuals against predicted values with quantile regression lines."
set.seed(42)
sim <- simulateResiduals(u_lmer_model, n = 1000)
plot(sim)
```

DHARMa **simulates** new data from your fitted model and checks the
real data against them. So the yardstick already includes the patches.
The same check works for `lmer`, `glmer`, Poisson and negative
binomial.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r lmm-diag-04}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
sim_patch <- recalculateResiduals(sim, group = u_df$patch)

data.frame(
  test = c("uniformity (QQ)", "dispersion", "outliers",
           "uniformity, by patch"),
  p    = round(c(testUniformity(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
                 testDispersion(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
                 testOutliers(sim, plot = FALSE)$p.value,
                 testUniformity(sim_patch, plot = FALSE)$p.value), 3))
```

::: callout-important
**The honest summary**

A **mild** departure from the expected distribution (percent cover
with lots of zeros), **no** dispersion problem, **no** outliers, and
nothing wrong at the level of the 16 patches.

Variances are also unequal across treatments (SD 3 at 100%, 29 at 0%).
Quinn & Keough found no transformation fixed it, analysed the raw data
and **said so**. Do the same.
:::
:::
::::::

## The Figure: Both Levels of Variation

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r linear-mixed-models-15}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-alt: "Model estimated marginal means with 95% confidence intervals by treatment, with the sixteen individual patch means plotted behind them, showing the patch means scatter widely within every treatment."
ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = raw_means, aes(treat, raw),
              width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.55, size = 2,
              color = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = as.data.frame(u_emm),
                  aes(treat, emmean, ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL),
                  color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8, size = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = "Urchin density treatment", y = "Algae cover (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Grey**: the 16 patch means. **Red**: the model's treatment means and
95% intervals.

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Read it as the model**

- The gap **between** red points is the treatment effect: big.
- The grey scatter **within** each treatment is the patch variance:
  also big.
- The treatment has to beat the grey scatter, and with 4 patches per
  treatment it can't quite.
:::
:::
:::::

## Reporting the Result

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: callout-note
**How to report this result**

"Algal cover did not differ significantly among urchin density
treatments (linear mixed model with patch as a random intercept,
***F*~3,12~ = 2.72, *p* = 0.091**, Kenward-Roger df), although cover
was much higher where urchins were removed (39%) than at natural
density (1%). Patches varied as much as quadrats within patches (patch
variance **294**, residual variance **299**, **ICC = 0.50**). Treatment
explained 24% of the variation in cover, and treatment plus patch 62%
(marginal R² = 0.24, conditional R² = 0.62)."
:::

**Both halves belong in the sentence.** The *F*-test answers *did the
treatment do anything*. The variance components answer *how variable
is this reef*, which is what the next person planning a study needs.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-important
**⚠️ "Not significant" is not "no effect"**

The effect is large. The design had only 4 patches per treatment
against a lot of patch-to-patch variation.

The honest conclusion is **"this design could not detect it, and more
patches would"**, not "urchins do not affect algae."
:::
:::
:::::

## Under the Hood (Optional)

::: {.compact-table}
| | **Nested ANOVA, `aov(Error())`** | **Mixed model, `lmer()`** |
|------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| How it gets the variances | splits sums of squares, solves for the variances | **REML**: searches for the variances that make the data most likely |
| Patch variance here | 294.3 | 294.3 |
| *F*-test for `treat` | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72, *p* = 0.091 | *F*~3,12~ = 2.72, *p* = 0.091 |
| Needs a balanced design? | **yes** | no |
| A variance can come out negative? | yes, which is meaningless | no, stops at 0 with a **"singular fit"** warning |
| Reports the variances and ICC? | no | **yes** |
:::

::: callout-note
**✅ The one sentence**

On a balanced design like this one the two methods agree exactly.
When patches have different numbers of quadrats, or there is more than
one grouping, only the mixed model still works. That is why it
replaced `Error()`.

The full story (the sums-of-squares table, the patch variance by hand,
REML written out, why `lme4` prints no *p*-values, and the bootstrap)
is in
[Mixed Models Under the Hood](../../vignettes/16_lmm_under_the_hood_vignette/lmm_under_the_hood.qmd).
:::

## Part 5 · The Same Factor, Fixed or Random: the Crayfish {.divider}

## Back to the Crayfish {.tight-code}

```{r lmm-cray-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
cray_df <- read_csv("data/sargent_lodge_crayfish.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(range = factor(range, levels = c("Native", "Invasive")),
         lake  = factor(lake,  levels = c("Big", "High", "Papoose")))

cray_cells <- cray_df %>%
  group_by(lake, range) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(growth_per_day), .groups = "drop")

cray_fixed <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range * lake, data = cray_df)
cray_add   <- lm(growth_per_day ~ range + lake, data = cray_df)
cray_ri    <- lmer(growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake), data = cray_df)
cray_rs    <- lmer(growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range),
                   data = cray_df)
```

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Sargent & Lodge (2014). Young rusty crayfish from the **Native** (Ohio)
and **Invasive** (Wisconsin) range, grown in enclosures in **three**
Wisconsin lakes. Response: `growth_per_day` (mm/day).

In the factorial weeks `lake` was **fixed**:

```{r lmm-cray-02}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
Anova(cray_fixed, type = 3)[2:4, ]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-03}
#| echo: false
#| collapse: true
cray_cells %>%
  dplyr::select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = range, values_from = mean) %>%
  mutate(advantage = Invasive - Native) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

::: callout-important
**The result you already know**

Invasive crayfish grew about **0.07** mm/day faster in Big and High,
and **not at all** faster in Papoose. The interaction *is* the finding:
the advantage is real in two lakes and absent in the third.

Today's question: what happens when `lake` becomes **random**?
:::
:::
:::::

## Fixed Lake or Random Lake? Two Different Questions

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.compact-table}
| | `lake` **fixed** | `lake` **random** |
|------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| The question | do **Big, High, Papoose** differ? | how much do **lakes** vary? |
| What R estimates | a mean for each lake | one **lake variance** |
| Post-hoc | Tukey: Big vs Papoose, etc. | none, no levels to compare |
| Conclusions are about | **these three lakes** | lakes **in general** |
:::

Neither is "the correct model". Pick the one that matches the sentence
you want to write in the Discussion.
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 Which did the authors mean?**

Sargent & Lodge did not care whether Big Lake differs from High Lake.
They wanted to know whether the invasive advantage holds in Wisconsin
lakes **generally**. That is a random-effect question.

The catch: they only had **three** lakes. Keep that number in view.
:::
::::
:::::::

## What the Random-Lake Model Says {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-04}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
cray_ri <- lmer(
  growth_per_day ~ range + (1 | lake),
  data = cray_df)

print(VarCorr(cray_ri),
      comp = c("Variance", "Std.Dev."))

icc(cray_ri)

emmeans(cray_ri, pairwise ~ range)$contrasts
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Read it exactly like the urchins:

- **`lake (Intercept)`**: the **lake variance**. Lakes typically sit
  ±0.063 mm/day from the average lake.
- **`Residual`**: the **residual variance**. Crayfish within a lake
  scatter ±0.035 mm/day.
- **ICC = 0.76**: three-quarters of the variation is between lakes.
- **Invasive − Native = 0.043 mm/day**, on **80 df**.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Notice the 80 df**

`range` varies **within** every lake, so this model counts every
crayfish as a replicate of the invasive advantage. Is that right? Next
slides.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Models, One Row Each {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-07}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
a_int <- Anova(cray_fixed, type = 3)["range", ]
a_add <- Anova(cray_add,   type = 3)["range", ]
a_ri  <- Anova(cray_ri, type = 3,
               test.statistic = "F")["range", ]

tibble(
  model = c("range * lake, fixed",
            "range + lake, fixed",
            "range + (1 | lake)"),
  F     = c(a_int$`F value`, a_add$`F value`, a_ri$F),
  df2   = c(df.residual(cray_fixed),
            df.residual(cray_add), a_ri$Df.res),
  p     = c(a_int$`Pr(>F)`, a_add$`Pr(>F)`,
            a_ri$`Pr(>F)`))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**The random intercept changed nothing about `range`**

The additive fixed model and the random-intercept model give the
**same test**: *F* = 27.6 on 1 and 80 df. Making `lake` random changed
how lake is **reported** (one variance, not two means), not the
*p*-value.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ And it quietly dropped the interaction**

The random-intercept model **is the additive model**. It assumes the
invasive advantage is the **same in every lake**.

The factorial weeks showed that is **false**: Papoose disagrees.
:::
:::
:::::

## Where Did the Interaction Go?

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-cray-08}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of growth per day against range with one line per lake. Left, random intercept only: three parallel lines. Right, random intercept and slope: Big and High rise steeply while Papoose is flat. Observed cell means are overlaid as points in both panels."
nd <- expand.grid(range = levels(cray_df$range),
                  lake  = levels(cray_df$lake))
nd$`(1 | lake)`                    <- predict(cray_ri, newdata = nd)
nd$`(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)` <- predict(cray_rs, newdata = nd)

nd %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(range, lake), names_to = "model", values_to = "fit") %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model, c("(1 | lake)",
                                 "(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(range, fit, group = lake, color = lake)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = cray_cells %>%
               tidyr::crossing(model = factor(c("(1 | lake)",
                                 "(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)"))),
             aes(y = mean), shape = 1, size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Growth (mm/day)", color = "Lake") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Open circles are the observed means. The left model can only move each
lake **up or down**, so it can't reach Papoose's two points.
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**`(1 | lake)` = parallel lines**

A random **intercept** gives every lake its own baseline and **nothing
else**. That is exactly "no interaction".
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Pseudoreplication, in a new costume**

What we want to generalise is *the invasive advantage in a lake*. That
was observed **three times**, once per lake. Yet the random-intercept
model tests it on **80 df**, as if every crayfish were a separate
lake.
:::
::::
:::::::

## A Random Slope: Each Lake Gets Its Own Advantage {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r lmm-cray-09}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
cray_rs <- lmer(
  growth_per_day ~ range +
    (1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range),
  data = cray_df)

VarCorr(cray_rs)

Anova(cray_rs, type = 3,
      test.statistic = "F")["range", ]
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`(1 | lake:range)` gives **each lake its own range effect**: a random
**slope**. It's the right-hand panel of the last slide.

- **`lake:range` SD 0.030**: how much the invasive advantage changes
  from lake to lake. The interaction, as a variance.
- ***F*~1,2~ = 3.3, *p* = 0.21.** The advantage is still about 0.046,
  but it is now tested on **2 df** (3 lakes − 1), not 80.

::: callout-important
**The yardstick changed**

`range` is now tested against **lake-to-lake disagreement** about the
advantage. One lake in three disagrees, so we can't say the advantage
holds in lakes generally.
:::

You may also see this written `(1 + range | lake)`. Same idea, one
extra parameter. See
[Mixed Model Structures](../../vignettes/16_mixed_model_structures_vignette/mixed_model_structures.qmd).
:::
:::::

## Which Analysis Is Right? Whichever Matches the Question

::: {.compact-table}
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Model                            | `range` *p*      | What you may write in the Discussion                       |
+==================================+==================+============================================================+
| `range * lake`, all fixed        | < 0.0001, **but  | "In Big and High Lake invasive crayfish grew ~0.07 mm/day  |
|                                  | the interaction  | faster; in Papoose they did not." Strong, specific, true,  |
|                                  | rules**          | **about these three lakes.**                               |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| `range + (1 | lake)`             | 0.000001         | "Invasive crayfish grow faster in lakes generally." Only   |
|                                  |                  | **by assuming the advantage is the same in every lake**,   |
|                                  |                  | which the data contradict. **Do not write this.**          |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
| `range + (1 | lake) +`           | 0.21             | "Across lakes generally, we cannot say the advantage       |
| `(1 | lake:range)`               |                  | holds: it appeared in two of three lakes." Honest but weak,|
|                                  |                  | because **three lakes is three replicates.**               |
+----------------------------------+------------------+------------------------------------------------------------+
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
**The mixed model's advantage is not a smaller *p***

It makes you **say what you are generalising to**, and then counts the
right replicates for that claim.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-warning
**⚠️ Three lakes is too few for a variance**

`confint(cray_ri)` puts the lake SD between **0.027 and 0.152**, a
six-fold range. With 16 patches the random effect was the right tool.
With 3 lakes, report the **fixed** model and say the general claim
rests on three lakes.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 5: The Short Version

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. A fixed factor gives you **its levels**. A random factor gives you
   **a variance**. Choose by the question.
2. `(1 | g)` means **parallel lines**: it assumes the treatment effect
   is the same in every group, and tests it on within-group df.
3. A random **slope**, `(1 | g) + (1 | g:x)`, lets the effect differ by
   group. It tests the treatment on **group** df.
4. **Below ~5 groups, fit the factor as fixed.**
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 In one sentence**

The mixed model did not change the crayfish result. It changed **who
the result is about**, and showed that the general claim rests on
three lakes, two of which agree.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6 · Two Designs You Will Actually Run {.divider}

## Animals Followed Through Time: Chick Growth

::::: columns
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{r lmm-chick-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-alt: "Body weight against age in days for fifty chicks, one line per chick, in four panels by diet. Lines start close together near forty grams and fan out with age; diet 3 chicks reach the highest weights."
ck_df <- as_tibble(ChickWeight) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(chick = factor(chick, ordered = FALSE))

ggplot(ck_df, aes(time, weight, group = chick)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ diet, nrow = 1, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Age (days)", y = "Body weight (g)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

`ChickWeight` ships with R: **50 chicks** on **4 diets**, each weighed
up to **12 times** over 21 days, 578 weighings.
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
The same structure as the urchins:

::: {.compact-table}
| Urchins | Chicks |
|------------------|------------------|
| treatment → patch | diet → chick |
| 5 quadrats per patch | 12 weighings per chick |
| 16 patches | 50 chicks |
:::

The diet was given to the **chick**. Twelve weighings of one chick are
not twelve chicks.

::: callout-note
**📖 What is new**

Each chick has its own **line**: its own starting weight **and** its
own growth rate. The lines **fan out**. So we need a random intercept
**and** a random slope for time:

`(1 + time | chick)`
:::
:::
:::::

## Each Chick Gets Its Own Growth Line {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
The question is `time:diet`: **do chicks grow at different rates on
different diets?**

```{r lmm-chick-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
ck_lm <- lm(weight ~ time * diet, data = ck_df)
ck_ri <- lmer(weight ~ time * diet + (1 | chick),
              data = ck_df)
ck_rs <- lmer(weight ~ time * diet + (1 + time | chick),
              data = ck_df)
```

```{r lmm-chick-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
a_lm <- car::Anova(ck_lm, type = 3)
a_ri <- anova(ck_ri)
a_rs <- anova(ck_rs)

data.frame(
  model   = c("lm, no chick", "(1 | chick)", "(1 + time | chick)"),
  F_value = round(c(a_lm["time:diet", "F value"],
                    a_ri["time:diet", "F value"],
                    a_rs["time:diet", "F value"]), 1),
  den_df  = round(c(a_lm["Residuals", "Df"],
                    a_ri["time:diet", "DenDF"],
                    a_rs["time:diet", "DenDF"])))
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: callout-important
**570 → 527 → 46 denominator df**

Only the last model knows there are **50 chicks**. Growth rate belongs
to a chick, so it has to be tested against **chick-to-chick
differences in growth rate**. Diet still matters (*p* = 0.002), on
honest df.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ The random intercept alone made it worse**

`(1 | chick)` gave the **largest** *F*. It still assumes every chick on
a diet grows at the **same rate**.

If a predictor's effect can differ among your animals, it needs the
**random slope**.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 How to choose**

Plot one line per animal. **Parallel** → random intercept.
**Fanning or crossing** → random slope.
:::
:::
:::::

## What the Chick Model Says {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r lmm-chick-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
VarCorr(ck_rs)

emtrends(ck_rs, ~ diet, var = "time") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::select(diet, time.trend, SE, df) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**1. The average growth rate on each diet** comes from `emtrends()`
(the `time.trend` column, which is `emmeans()` for slopes):

- diet 1: **6.3** g/day · diet 2: **8.6** · diet 3: **11.4** · diet 4:
  **9.5**
- each SE rests on about **45 df**: the chicks, not the 578 weighings.

**2. How much chicks vary around that average** comes from `VarCorr()`:

- **`time` SD 3.3**: chicks on the *same* diet differ in growth rate by
  about **3.3 g/day**. On diet 1, a typical chick grows somewhere
  between about **3 and 10 g/day** (6.3 ± 3.3). Individuals vary a lot.
- **Residual SD 12.8**: one weighing sits about 13 g off that chick's
  own line.
- **Corr −0.98**: don't interpret it. Growth curves upward, so a
  straight line through a fast grower starts too low.

**Your own repeated measures** (tagged fish, resurveyed plots, repeat
blood samples) use the same model: `(1 + time | id)`.
:::
:::::

## A Treatment Blocked by Stream

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-01}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: "Insects per sample on a log scale for three reach types, reference, willow and removed, in three panels, one per stream. Grey dots are the fifteen samples in each reach and blue diamonds joined by a line are the nine reach means. All three streams drop from reference to willow, but the streams sit at different overall levels."
w_df <- read_csv("data/willow_streams_simulated.csv",
                 show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(reach  = factor(reach, levels = c("reference", "willow", "removed")),
         stream = factor(stream),
         log_insects = log(insects))

w_means <- w_df %>%
  group_by(stream, reach) %>%
  summarise(log_insects = mean(log_insects), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(w_df, aes(reach, log_insects)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey55", alpha = 0.6, size = 1,
             position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
  geom_line(data = w_means, aes(group = stream), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(data = w_means, colour = "#0072B2", size = 3, shape = 18) +
  facet_wrap(~ stream, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log(insects per sample)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 10) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**3 streams.** In each: a **reference** reach, a reach with **crack
willow**, and a reach where willow was **removed**. **15 samples** per
reach, 135 in all.

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ These data are simulated**

The layout is a real student project. The numbers are made up, so we
know the truth: willow cuts insects by 30%.
:::

::: callout-important
**The giveaway question again**

*What was the treatment applied to?* A **reach**. There are **9**
reaches (the blue diamonds), only **3 of each kind**.

The 15 samples are the quadrats. The reach is the patch. The stream is
a **block**.
:::
:::
:::::

## Three Analyses of the Same 135 Samples {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-02}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_naive <- lm(log_insects ~ reach, data = w_df)
w_fixed <- lm(log_insects ~ reach * stream, data = w_df)
w_mixed <- lmer(
  log_insects ~ reach + (1 | stream) + (1 | stream:reach),
  data = w_df,
  control = lmerControl(calc.derivs = FALSE))
```

```{r lmm-stream-03}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_a1 <- anova(w_naive)
w_a2 <- anova(w_fixed)
w_a3 <- anova(w_mixed)

data.frame(
  model   = c("reach only", "reach * stream, fixed", "mixed"),
  F_value = round(c(w_a1["reach", "F value"], w_a2["reach", "F value"],
                    w_a3["reach", "F value"]), 2),
  den_df  = round(c(w_a1["Residuals", "Df"], w_a2["Residuals", "Df"],
                    w_a3["reach", "DenDF"])),
  p       = format.pval(c(w_a1["reach", "Pr(>F)"], w_a2["reach", "Pr(>F)"],
                          w_a3["reach", "Pr(>F)"]), digits = 1, eps = 0.0001))
```

**The effect was real.** We built in a 30% drop and got *p* = 0.10.
Three streams is three replicates. More samples per reach would not
have helped.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**4 denominator df, not 132**

- `(1 | stream:reach)` gives each of the 9 reaches its own offset. It
  is the urchin `(1 | patch)`.
- `(1 | stream)` is the block.

Reach is tested against how much the willow effect **changes from
stream to stream**: (3 − 1) × (3 − 1) = 4 df.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ All-fixed looks careful but is the worst**

`reach * stream` gives the biggest *F*. It tests reach against
sample-to-sample noise, as if the 15 samples were 15 reaches.
:::
:::
:::::

## Stream: Fixed Block or Random Block? {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r lmm-stream-04}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
# stream as a FIXED block, reach still random
w_block <- lmer(
  log_insects ~ reach + stream + (1 | stream:reach),
  data = w_df)

# the old way: analyse the 9 reach means
w_rcb <- lm(log_insects ~ reach + stream, data = w_means)
```

```{r lmm-stream-05}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| collapse: true
w_a4 <- anova(w_block)
w_a5 <- anova(w_rcb)

data.frame(
  model   = c("stream random", "stream fixed block", "9 reach means"),
  F_value = round(c(w_a3["reach", "F value"], w_a4["reach", "F value"],
                    w_a5["reach", "F value"]), 2),
  den_df  = round(c(w_a3["reach", "DenDF"], w_a4["reach", "DenDF"],
                    w_a5["Residuals", "Df"])),
  p       = round(c(w_a3["reach", "Pr(>F)"], w_a4["reach", "Pr(>F)"],
                    w_a5["reach", "Pr(>F)"]), 3))
```

Identical. For the **reach** test on a balanced design it does not
matter whether the block is fixed or random.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**What is not optional is `(1 | stream:reach)`**

Drop it and the 15 samples become replicates again. Whatever you do
with the stream, the **reach** must be in the model as a random term,
or you analyse the 9 reach means.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Which to report with 3 streams**

Same answer as the crayfish: **stream as a fixed block**. Three streams
can't pin down a variance; a random block often comes back as exactly 0
with a *singular fit* warning.

With 6 or more streams, make it random and report the variance.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 6: The Short Version

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. **Repeated measures on an animal** are subsamples of that animal.
   Put the animal in the random part, and put **time on the left of the
   bar** if animals can differ in their rate of change.
2. A random **intercept alone** can make things worse: it still treats
   every measurement as a replicate of the slope.
3. **Blocked treatments with subsamples** need the treated unit as a
   random term, `(1 | stream:reach)`, whatever you do with the block.
4. With fewer than about 5 blocks, fit the block as **fixed**.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-note
**📖 In one sentence**

Before fitting anything, ask **what the treatment was applied to** and
count those. That number, not the number of rows, sets the denominator
df, and `lmer()` gets it right only if that unit is in the model.
:::

::: callout-tip
**🖐 Counts, not logs**

Insect counts really want a Poisson or negative binomial response:
`glmer.nb(insects ~ reach + stream + (1 | stream:reach))`. Same random
part; last week's distribution.
:::
:::
:::::

## Part 7 · Wrap-Up {.divider}

## The `lmer` Formula Cheat-Sheet

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="58%"}
Read every random term as **`( what varies | across which groups )`**.

::: {.compact-table}
| Formula | Say it aloud | Picture |
|------------------|---------------------------|----------------|
| `(1 | patch)` | "the intercept differs among patches" | parallel lines |
| `(1 | treat:patch)` | same, naming patch-within-treatment | parallel lines |
| `(1 + time | chick)` | "the intercept **and** the slope of time differ among chicks" | lines fan out |
| `(1 | lake) + (1 | lake:range)` | each lake gets its own baseline and its own range effect | lines cross |
| `(1 | a) + (1 | b)` | two **crossed** random factors | every a meets every b |
| `(1 | a/b)` | b **nested** in a: shorthand for `(1 | a) + (1 | a:b)` | b lives inside one a |
:::

The right side of the bar must be a **grouping factor**. A predictor
can go on the left only if it **varies within** the groups: urchin
density doesn't vary within a patch, so `(1 + treat | patch)` can't be
fitted.
::::

:::: {.column width="42%"}
::: callout-tip
**🖐 Do I need `a/b` or `a:b`?**

Only if the inner IDs **restart** inside each outer level (patch 1–4
in *every* treatment). Our patches are numbered 1–16, so `(1 | patch)`
already says it.
:::

::: callout-warning
**⚠️ "boundary (singular) fit"**

A variance came out as **exactly 0**: there wasn't enough information
to estimate it (usually too few groups). Simplify the random effects;
don't ignore the warning.
:::
::::
:::::::

## The Six Lines You Need {.tight-code}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
``` r
# 1. fit: grouping in the random part
m <- lmer(algae ~ treat + (1 | patch), data = u_df)

# 2. read the two variances
summary(m)

# 3. share of variation among patches, and R²
icc(m)
r2(m)

# 4. test the treatment (report this one)
Anova(m, type = 3, test.statistic = "F")

# 5. treatment means and comparisons
emmeans(m, ~ treat) %>% pairs()

# 6. check it
plot(simulateResiduals(m))
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-important
**✅ The one idea to keep**

A mixed model doesn't "remove" the patch effect. It **estimates** it
(the patch variance and the ICC) and tests the treatment against the
right amount of noise.
:::

Today you:

- found the **real replicate** by asking what got the treatment
- read the **patch** and **residual** variances
- used the **ICC** to see that more patches, not more quadrats, was
  the fix
- reported the ***F*-test** and both variances
- saw the same logic on **lakes**, **chicks** and **streams**

::: callout-note
**📖 Up next**

`glmer()`: a non-normal response **and** a random effect. You now have
both halves.
:::
:::
:::::

## Before Next Class

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
Take the pine needle data, **collapsed to one value per team per side**
(the two-stage summary from Week 3):

``` r
p_df <- pine_df |>
  group_by(team, side) |>
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

anova(lmer(needle_length_mm ~ side + (1|team), data = p_df))
```

Compare *F* to the **square of** the paired-*t* statistic from Week 4
(*t* = −2.72). You should get ***F* = 7.41, df 1 and 3, *p* = 0.072**:
the paired *t*-test **is** this mixed model.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early**

Run the same formula on the **raw 64 needles**. You get *p* = 0.057 on
**59** denominator df, not 3, because `(1|team)` alone assumes `side`
behaves identically in every team, so all 64 needles count as
replicates of the side effect. (Sound familiar? It's the crayfish
problem.)
:::
:::
